first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are funnel-internal (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a single onboarding intervention plausibly moves both. The competitor's entry pricing is real, but promotional_pricing (memory_73) is the direction most likely to buy short-term acquisition at the cost of the stated objective: discount-acquired price-sensitive SMB accounts tend to carry weaker expansion and retention, and memory_73's summary reports 'acquisition and revenue lift' without any horizon or margin qualifier, so it does not actually evidence sustainable qualified revenue. Referral (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) address neither declining metric this week. I am spending the single verification on memory_86 rather than on the pricing memory because memory_86 is the load-bearing support for what I intend to do, and its summary is stated entirely in leading proxies — 'completion rates', 'time-to-value', 'early product adoption' — none of which are qualified revenue. I want the original record to tell me the measurement window, whether retention or revenue was tracked at all past week one, and what was actually removed from the flow. The specific downstream risk I am flagging: memory_31's mechanism was cutting required signup fields, which improves activation partly by lowering the qualification bar. That can raise activation counts while degrading lead quality, routing, and eventual qualified revenue, and a summary that only reports activation would look identical in both worlds. These consolidated summaries have also lost their original effect sizes, sample sizes, and segments, and conditions have shifted since day 12-61 given the new competitor, so I treat all six as directional priors rather than settled facts. Hence a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout: instrument it with downstream qualified-revenue and lead-quality holdouts, not just completion and week-one activation, and preserve the ability to reverse. If the archive shows memory_86's lift was measured only on short-horizon proxies or came from removing genuine qualification signal, I will narrow the change to non-qualifying friction only, or shift the slot toward activation_messaging (memory_91), which improves engagement without lowering the entry bar.

final.rationale: The archive materially strengthened memory_86 in the specific way I was worried about. My concern was that the summary reported only leading proxies, which would look identical whether the change created real value or merely lowered the bar. The source record includes 30-day retention +3% alongside completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days, which is a genuine downstream check: accounts stayed, not just entered. It also clarifies the mechanism as a shortened flow, which is distinct from memory_31's cutting of required signup fields. That distinction matters, because field-removal is the variant that risks degrading lead qualification and routing, while step-reduction mainly removes friction. I am therefore designing the test as step and sequence reduction and explicitly not stripping qualifying fields, so I inherit memory_86's verified mechanism rather than memory_31's unverified one. This still targets both declining metrics, since onboarding sits upstream of activation, and it does not mortgage margin the way a discount response to the competitor would. I am upgrading from a small guarded test to a standard experiment because verification came back clean on a downstream metric, but not to broad rollout, because real gaps remain: 30-day retention is still not qualified revenue over a meaningful horizon, the record gives no sample size or segment breakdown, and day-76 conditions differ from the original run now that a competitor is actively pulling price-sensitive SMB accounts. Composition effects could differ from the original population. Guardrails: hold out a control, instrument downstream qualified-revenue and lead-quality alongside completion and week-one activation, monitor sales-accepted rates so a self-serve improvement is not quietly cannibalizing the demo-request path that memory_44 says works better for enterprise, and keep the change reversible. I am deliberately not treating the competitor pricing threat as unaddressed-but-ignored: promotional_pricing remains the direction most likely to inflate near-term acquisition while diluting the sustainable qualified revenue that is the actual objective, and memory_73 offers no horizon or margin evidence to overturn that. If this experiment's qualified-revenue holdout comes back flat despite completion and activation rising, that is the signal that the funnel gains are not converting to value, and the next slot should go to activation_messaging (memory_91) or a properly instrumented pricing test rather than more onboarding work.
